content: The ABCG5 and ABCG8 genes encode two proteins known as sterolin-1 and sterolin-2, respectively. These proteins are classified as half ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters and are essential for regulating the absorption and excretion of sterols. Mutations in either of these genes lead to a lipid disorder called sitosterolemia. The molecular mechanisms that govern the absorption of dietary sterols in the body remain poorly understood. Sitosterolemia is a rare autosomal recessive lipid metabolic disorder characterized by excessive absorption and reduced biliary excretion of dietary sterols. Research into the molecular basis of sitosterolemia has provided insights into the processes of intestinal sterol absorption and cholesterol secretion into bile. In 1998, the genetic locus for sitosterolemia (STSL) was mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 2 (2p21) after studying 10 well-characterized families with the disorder. By 2001, the STSL locus was found to include two genes, ABCG5 and ABCG8, which encode sterolin-1 and sterolin-2, respectively. Sterolin-2 was discovered after sterolin-1 and is located less than 400 base pairs upstream of sterolin-1 in the opposite orientation. The proteins encoded by these genes belong to the ABC transporter family. A typical ABC transporter consists of two transmembrane domains and two nucleotide-binding domains. However, members of the ABCG (or White) subfamily, which includes five fully characterized human proteins, are half-size ABC proteins that likely dimerize to form functional membrane transporters. In the case of ABCG5 and ABCG8, it is suggested that they form a heterodimer. These half-size ABCG proteins have a unique domain organization, with a nucleotide-binding domain at the N-terminus followed by six transmembrane-spanning domains. Under normal conditions, a Western diet contains nearly equal amounts of cholesterol and non-cholesterol sterols (such as plant sterols like sitosterol, campesterol, and brassicasterol). However, only about 55% of dietary cholesterol is absorbed and retained, while almost none of the non-cholesterol sterols are retained. The small amount of dietary non-cholesterol sterols that enter the body is rapidly excreted by the liver into bile, largely unchanged. Sterolins are believed to play a role in the selective transport of dietary cholesterol into and out of enterocytes and in the selective excretion of sterols by the liver into bile. This is supported by the consequences observed when sterolins are deficient or overexpressed. The precise mechanisms by which ABCG5 and ABCG8 influence sterol metabolism remain unclear. However, it is hypothesized that the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimer facilitates the transport of cholesterol from the inner leaflet of the canalicular membrane through a chamber formed by the two half-transporters. Following ATP binding and hydrolysis, the complex undergoes a conformational change, flipping a cholesterol molecule into the outer membrane leaflet in a configuration that promotes its release into the canalicular space. Based on clinical findings in sitosterolemia, ABCG5 and ABCG8 are expressed in the liver and/or intestine. These genes respond to environmental dietary sterols, although it is not yet determined whether they are also upregulated by high levels of phytosterols. It is worth noting that other gene products, such as ABCA1, also play a role in dietary cholesterol transport. Mutations in both alleles of either the ABCG5 or ABCG8 gene result in sitosterolemia. Sitosterolemia, also known as phytosterolemia, is a rare autosomal recessive lipid metabolic disorder. It is characterized by the presence of tendon xanthomas, premature coronary artery disease, atherosclerotic disease, hemolytic episodes, arthralgias, and arthritis. The hallmark of sitosterolemia is diagnostically elevated levels of plant sterols in the plasma.
